Where Does Gold Really Hide in a Stream? 7 Prospecting Rules Worth Questioning

Gold Trails · Research & river reading · Published October 27, 2026

A promising bend, a stubborn clay layer, a handsome crack in bedrock: each can make you feel that the next pan ought to be the one. The trouble begins when a useful clue becomes an instruction to stop thinking.

Prospecting rules are good starting questions. They become much more useful when you ask what produced the sediment, how water moved it, and what an actual sample tells you. Here are seven familiar shortcuts worth slowing down for.

Evidence note: Creator observations below come from attributed, timestamped research notes retained in our library. The cited video moments are caption-derived anchors; we have not independently reviewed their audio or footage. They are reported observations and hypotheses, not verified assays or controlled experiments. Geological publications support the specific background statements beside their links. The suggested field comparisons are Gold Trails’ editorial recommendations.

In this article
  1. The inside bend is always the best place
  2. Just dig behind the biggest boulder
  3. Nothing counts until you reach solid bedrock
  4. Hardpan and clay mean the same thing everywhere
  5. A pan full of black sand proves gold is nearby
  6. The gold-bearing channel must be where today’s water is
  7. One poor pan means the whole spot is finished

Watch as you read: The creator links beside each example open YouTube at the recorded timestamp in a separate window, leaving this article open. Your browser may choose a tab instead. These links identify the research anchors; their precise spoken context still needs audio review.

1. The inside bend is always the best place

An inside bend gives you a sensible place to begin. Warren E. Yeend’s USGS placer-gold model includes inside meanders among several depositional settings. It also names other settings. The model is a description of deposits, not a promise about the bend in front of you.

In the retained notes for Northeast Expanse’s Vermont outing, at 12:30, the creator reasons about a middle-of-bend target instead of automatically choosing the inside. That is an example of asking a different question, not proof that the middle is better: the flow was not measured and the comparison was not controlled.

Another useful counterexample comes from Vo-Gus Prospecting: our imported notes describe an inside bend with bare bedrock and almost no deposited gravel. Watch the recorded example at 1:50. His rejection of that particular bend and Northeast Expanse’s interest in a different position are compatible with looking for sediment that actually stayed put. Differences in scour, fractures, and retained gravel could explain the choices; neither account establishes a universal winning position.

Try this: Where access and conditions permit, compare separately labeled samples from a few positions. Record the layer and starting volume. “Inside bend” is a location description; the recovered material supplies the result.

2. Just dig behind the biggest boulder

The attractive part of a boulder is that it gives your eye something to organize the river around. It still leaves questions: which flow direction matters, where is the sediment contact, and is that rock safely stable?

Our caption-derived notes record Northeast Expanse reporting a previously productive boulder spot, at 3:15. The account does not compare that position with equally sized samples from the upstream side or flanks. It supports investigating that particular spot, not ranking every side of every boulder.

Yeend’s deposit model includes concentrations beneath boulders. That geological observation is not an instruction to excavate underneath one.

Try this: Compare safely accessible sediment beside an obstruction with nearby control gravel. Never undermine a boulder, excavate an unstable bank, or enter dangerous current to complete a comparison.

3. Nothing counts until you reach solid bedrock

Bedrock matters, but the first useful boundary may lie above it. Yeend describes gold concentrations within gravel above clay layers, where the clay constrains downward movement. A compact layer deserves a description and a sample; it does not automatically deserve either the name bedrock or the label pay dirt.

There are competing ideas about the rock itself, too. In the saved caption notes for Two Toes at 1:00, rock durability is offered as an explanation for how long a crack might persist. That is a hypothesis about trap history. Without comparable samples, it cannot establish that harder rock yields more gold.

Dan Hurd offers a complementary explanation in his bedrock lesson: the imported notes say clay can intercept settling gold above solid rock. See his discussion at 7:30. This differs in emphasis from Two Toes’ durable-crack hypothesis, rather than disproving it. One concerns a compact sediment contact; the other concerns a rock fissure. Which boundary matters at your site remains a sampling question.

Try this: Keep overlying gravel, contact material, and any safely accessible lower material separate. Avoid blending them into a bucket that leaves you unable to tell which layer supplied the gold. Our bedrock-map guide explains why a mapped rock boundary is another clue with limits.

4. Hardpan and clay mean the same thing everywhere

This shortcut is particularly troublesome in New England. Similar-looking resistant material can have different origins. D. G. Woodward’s 1984 USGS description of Minnesota’s buried glacial deposits distinguishes unsorted till containing clay, silt, sand, and gravel from stratified sand-and-gravel deposits. It is a Minnesota aquifer study, not a placer-gold survey, but the sediment distinction is useful.

The Maine Geological Survey explains that Maine gold occurs in bedrock, glacier-eroded sediments, and stream deposits derived from either. The history of a loose stone can therefore be more complicated than erosion from the nearest outcrop.

The library’s notes for Minerals, Rocks, and Fossil Talks, at 7:30 flag an overly broad account of where clay occurs. Woodward’s description supplies a concrete counterexample: till can contain clay. That does not invalidate an entire video; it identifies a statement requiring qualification.

Try this: Write down what you can observe—sorting, grain sizes, layering, packing—before deciding whether a deposit is till, outwash, or river gravel. A geological map or survey description can help; appearance alone need not settle it.

5. A pan full of black sand proves gold is nearby

Black sand is worth examining. It is not a gold count. Harold Kirkemo, William L. Newman, and Roger P. Ashley’s USGS overview of gold describes magnetite and other heavy minerals in black-sand concentrates. Identifying those minerals and identifying gold remain separate tasks.

Our interpretation is modest: a heavy-mineral concentrate can help you decide what to investigate next, but cannot establish the amount of gold in the starting gravel. A bigger dark grain is not a calibrated prediction of a bigger nugget.

The creator evidence here concerns cleanup, not proof that dark gravel is rich. In the retained caption notes, Dan Hurd warns that a magnet plunged into Fraser River concentrates can carry fine gold along with magnetic sand. Watch his warning at 6:30. Au77 explores a different arrangement: magnets beneath a dry pan. See the recorded experiment at 3:30. The notes describe magnetic sand being retained while gold moves through gaps, but do not establish how much gold remains in the rejects.

These accounts should not be reduced to “magnets work” versus “magnets fail.” Dry material, magnet placement, and particle entanglement are different conditions that could affect separation. Neither example measures the original gravel’s gold grade. Evidence gap: the selected notes do not provide a controlled comparison connecting black-sand abundance with gold yield.

Try this: Make two notes: what the dark concentrate looks like, and what gold you actually identify. Retain uncertain material for another look rather than filling the gap with a hopeful estimate. Our black-sands article takes that distinction through cleanup.

6. The gold-bearing channel must be where today’s water is

Old river deposits can survive above a modern channel. Peterson, Yeend, Oliver, and Mattick’s 1968 study of gold-bearing channel gravels in northern Nevada County, California documents ancient channel deposits along a ridge between the South and Middle Yuba River canyons.

That is a documented regional example. It does not mean every elevated patch of gravel is an ancient gold channel.

In our caption-derived notes, Ask Jeff Williams discusses a proposed old-channel remnant at 1:30. Its age and identification remain questions for geological mapping and source review. The Yuba study is a separate example, not verification of the location in his video.

Try this: Treat elevated gravel as a research lead. Check the mapped deposit and its history before assigning an age, source, or gold content. Do not climb or cut an unstable exposure to test a theory.

7. One poor pan means the whole spot is finished

A disappointing result belongs in the notebook. It describes one sample and your recovery from it; it does not automatically describe the entire reach.

The retained notes record Northeast Expanse reporting little gold after many pans, at 16:30. In another outing, 911 EXPLORATION CORP reports several positive pans, with differing results, at 3:57. These are different places and qualitative accounts. They are not a fair experiment showing that one trap, region, or method wins.

Try this: Repeat a promising or puzzling sample using a comparable starting volume and processing method. Keep zero results, spills, and uncertain identifications distinct. There is no universal number of pans that proves a deposit. Our test-pan comparison guide offers a practical recording routine.

Give your next pan a better question

You do not need to abandon river-reading advice. Give it a smaller, testable job. Instead of deciding that a bend must hold gold, ask which accessible sediment position you will compare with which other one.

Record the deposit’s likely origin, the layer, the sample volume, the processing method, and the actual outcome. Keep an observation separate from its explanation. A blank pan can narrow a question; an exciting pan can suggest the next one. Neither has to become a story about an entire river.

Before sampling, confirm landowner permission, claim status, current local rules, and permitted methods. A video location, geological publication, or attractive trap does not grant access. Protect vegetation and banks, and choose observations you can make safely.

Sources and research scope

  • Warren E. Yeend, Descriptive model of Placer Au–PGE, model 39a, in USGS Bulletin 1693 (1986). Sections on depositional environments and ore controls.
  • Harold Kirkemo, William L. Newman, and Roger P. Ashley, Gold, USGS web edition. Placer deposits and black-sand minerals.
  • D. G. Woodward, The study of buried drift aquifers in Minnesota by seismic geophysical methods (1984), USGS Open-File Report, DOI 10.3133/70175429. Publisher abstract inspected; a full digital report was not linked on the record.
  • Maine Geological Survey, Gold in Maine, page updated April 12, 2023. Geological-origin paragraph used here; its regulations are not reproduced as a current legal checklist.
  • D. W. Peterson, W. E. Yeend, H. W. Oliver, and R. E. Mattick, Tertiary gold-bearing channel gravel in northern Nevada County, California (1968), USGS Circular 566, DOI 10.3133/cir566. Publisher abstract inspected.
